items.abstract: <jats:p>The subsistence economy of Early Iron Age communities in the Lower Danube remains insufficiently documented despite the large number of settlements attributed to the Babadag culture. This study examines subsistence practices at the eponymous Babadag settlement by combining archaeozoological, carpological, phytolith, and radiocarbon evidence from legacy excavation materials. The chronological framework includes 14 radiocarbon determinations, which broadly support an occupation between the end of the 11th/beginning of the 10th century BC and mid-8th century BC. The analysed assemblages comprise 11,475 faunal remains, two samples of charred plant macroremains, and nine sediment samples for phytolith analysis. Domestic mammals dominate the faunal assemblage, especially cattle and sheep/goat, with fishing providing an important supplementary food resource while hunting remained limited. Age-at-death data, together with the limited sex-ratio evidence, are consistent with mixed livestock exploitation, which may have included meat production, dairying, traction, wool production, and reproduction. Carpological remains document hulled barley, emmer, spelt wheat, and common millet, while phytoliths indicate repeated inputs of grass material into archaeological deposits. Overall, the evidence indicates a diversified subsistence economy based primarily on animal husbandry and cereal cultivation and processing, supplemented by fishing and the limited use of wild resources.</jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Dental plates are pivotal in the lungfish paleontological record, constituting highly mineralized structures resilient to diagenetic processes. This study provides a detailed description and quantitative shape analysis of 95 newly discovered
                    <jats:italic>Gnathorhiza</jats:italic>
                    sp. dental plates from the Middle–Late Permian Corumbataí Formation, Brazil. The analyzed sample comprises both upper and lower dentition morphotypes, sharing diagnostic generic features such as straight, sharp, and narrow conical ridges, an obtuse angle between the first and last ridges, a slightly conical lingual border, deep sulci, and an occlusal surface displaying reticulated ornamentation with distinct petrodentine cores. Taphonomic systematization suggests distinct preservation histories for each morphotype, explaining the overrepresentation of upper plates relative to lower ones. To quantitatively evaluate structural variation, landmark‐based geometric morphometrics was applied to both upper and lower tooth plates; however, due to a significantly larger sample size, the upper dentition yielded the most robust and biologically significant results. The geometric morphometric analyses revealed substantial morphological variance, particularly localized in the first ridge and first sulcus of the upper plates. Rather than resulting from strict ontogenetic developmental paths or sexual dimorphism, we hypothesize that these predominant morphological differences reflect high phenotypic plasticity within this isolated population. This study confirms the high abundance of
                    <jats:italic>Gnathorhiza</jats:italic>
                    in the Corumbataí Formation, provides a rigorous assessment of key morphological features in late Paleozoic dipnoan dental plates, and offers insights into the population dynamics of these specialized durophagous predators within a complex Permian mega‐lake paleoenvironment.
                  </jats:p>
authors: Mauro B. S. Lacerda, Gustavo H. N. Petreca, Gabriel E. B. de Barros, Ana Emilia Quezado, Marcelo A. Fernandes

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Fossil resins preserve not only body fossils but also a diverse record of trace fossils reflecting organism–substrate interactions during and after resin secretion. This study develops an ichnological framework for resin‐hosted traces, distinguishing between borings preserved on resin surfaces and behaviour‐related structures caught within the resin matrix, termed ichnoinclusions. The analysis is based on comprehensive sample of fossil resin material, including Baltic, Lublin, Ethiopian, Mexican (simojovelite) and Lebanese ambers. The documented ichnofossils represent multiple ichnofacies and record successive stages of resin taphonomy. Woodground‐related borings (e.g.
                    <jats:italic>Teredolites</jats:italic>
                    ,
                    <jats:italic>Apectoichnus</jats:italic>
                    ) are associated with early stages of resin accumulation, whereas lithic‐type borings assigned to
                    <jats:italic>Gastrochaenolites</jats:italic>
                     isp. reflect later phases of redeposition, burial and substrate induration. These observations demonstrate that fossil resin does not represent a single ichnotaxobase, but passes through a succession of substrate conditions, recording a multi‐stage ichnological history. In addition, ichnoinclusions provide independent taphonomic information. Structures such as silk threads, spider webs, larval cases, and frass accumulations record resin viscosity, flow dynamics and microenvironmental conditions at the moment of entrapment. The results support a taphonomic model linking ichnofacies succession with resin redeposition and demonstrate that fossil resins should be treated as dynamic substrates recording both biological activity and sedimentary processes.
                  </jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    We have investigated fine‐grained marine sediments buried under delta sediments and multiple till beds in a tributary valley in western Norway. The marine bed contains bivalves, foraminifera and terrestrial plant material. The fauna and flora are rather poor, but the presence of molluscan species
                    <jats:italic>Mytilus edulis</jats:italic>
                    and
                    <jats:italic>Arctica islandica</jats:italic>
                    suggests that Atlantic waters reached the coastal areas at the time of deposition. The age range of radiocarbon dates from about 25 to 50 ka BP conflicts with previous studies from the area and is considered as minimum ages only. This conclusion is supported by amino acid epimerization values in molluscs from the radiocarbon‐dated unit, indicating that it should be correlated with an Early Weichselian, MIS 5c interstadial. The marine unit and overlying delta succession are situated on the outer coast up to 56 m above present sea level, suggesting that they were deposited during a high sea‐level stand following retreat of an extensive MIS 5d glaciation. A compiled Weichselian glaciation curve shows five major glacial advances extending to the outermost coast or beyond. These advances seem to correspond to periods with North Atlantic sea surface cooling. Three till units on top of the delta are interpreted to represent glacier advance prior to the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) and during the subsequent deglaciation. Clast fabrics in the lower till and orientation of clastic dikes show an upvalley component opposite to LGM maximum ice‐flow direction. This indicates that initial glacier advance was by fjord glaciers extending to the outer coast while there was limited glacier extent in coastal mountain areas. This interpretation favours fast ice flow along the fjords and major supply of ice from interior mountain areas. Glacier growth in coastal mountains led to merging with fjord glaciers, reorientation of the ice‐flow direction and ultimately maximum glacier extent. Empirical data on ice‐sheet growth are extremely rare and may have been overlooked in many stratigraphic records. Such data are vital for understanding behaviour of ice sheets and in a wider sense, the climate system.
                  </jats:p>
authors: Eiliv Larsen, Hans Petter Sejrup, Brent Ward, William E. N. Austin, Hilary H. Birks, Oddvar Longva, Astrid Lyså, Dag Ottesen, Bente Philippsen, Martin Seiler
